questions.q: What two fields does the lesson say a standard classical docstring is missing for a quantum circuit-construction function?
options: Parameter names and return type
Function name and module path
Expected measurement distribution and which backend/SDK version the behavior was validated against
License and author name
questions.explain: The lesson argues classical-style Args/Returns documentation is necessary but not sufficient -- quantum functions additionally need to document the expected measurement distribution and which backend(s)/SDK version(s) that claim was actually validated against.

questions.q: In the improved GHZ circuit docstring example, why does it point to a specific test file (tests/test_ghz.py::test_ghz_statistical_distribution) rather than just describing the distribution in prose?
options: To give a reader a direct link between the documented claim and the executable test that actually validates it
Because docstrings are not allowed to contain prose descriptions
Because pytest requires docstrings to reference test files
It's purely stylistic and has no functional purpose
questions.explain: Pointing to the specific statistical test that validates the claimed distribution lets a reader verify the claim is actually enforced in the test suite, not just asserted in a comment that could go stale.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say a bare assertion like `assert z_score < 3` without documentation is a maintenance problem?
options: Because Python cannot execute that assertion
Because it tells a future maintainer nothing about why that threshold was chosen or what changing the shot count would do to it
Because z-scores are never used in quantum testing
Because assertions must always use <= instead of <
questions.explain: Without documenting the reasoning (confidence level, what range of phat the threshold tolerates at a given shot count), a future maintainer has no way to judge whether changing shots or the circuit requires revisiting the threshold.

questions.q: According to the lesson, what should a quantum package's README.md include that a typical classical library's README might not need to emphasize as strongly?
options: A full copy of every function's docstring
The specific SDK(s) and version(s) the package targets, plus a link to which real hardware backends it has actually been validated against
The founder's biography
A complete history of every git commit
questions.explain: Because quantum SDKs are pinned tightly (Chapter 3) and real-hardware behavior can differ from simulators, the lesson recommends the README state target SDK versions and link to hardware-validation documentation -- information a user needs before trusting results on their own account.

questions.q: In the docstring template table, what is the purpose of the 'Qubit roles' field?
options: To document the circuit's total runtime in seconds
To state which qubit indices play which logical role, such as which are the oracle's input register versus an ancilla
To list which programming language the circuit was written in
To record the git commit hash of the last edit
questions.explain: The 'Qubit roles' field exists specifically to tell a reader which qubit indices serve which logical purpose (e.g. input register vs. ancilla), information that isn't obvious from reading gate-application code alone.
